sources.title: Meta’s ‘Joyful’ Muse Charm May Cost a Not-So-Joyful $300 - Gizmodo
passages: That hardware, in case you missed it, is called Muse Charm , and it is, by CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s own description, “a joyful little device for talking to your Muse that fits on your keychain.” Despite how bad Meta seemingly wants you to use Muse, though, it may not wind up leading with a price that screams “buy me.”
According to a report from The Information , Meta is targeting a $300 price tag for the Muse Charm, which is (in this economy and most others) a sizeable amount of money.
Back in the day—just a couple of years ago, really—$300 used to get you a whole Xbox , though the RAM shortage has made those times feel like a dream you were sad to wake up from.
While some of you may be reading this and thinking, “Wow, Muse Charm sounds like a bad deal,” I can almost assure you Meta doth protest.
If you were waiting for a Meta-made alternative to the Apple Watch, that stinks.
Meta initially said that it was targeting a release around the holidays, so I guess you should start saving up to gift this expensive little charm to the favorite AI builder in your life.
Despite having an alleged price, the official details of what Muse Charm really does are scant.

extraction.body: Meta wants you to use its AI agent, Muse —like, bad. Really bad. Meta wants you to use Muse so bad, in fact, that it’s making hardware with a cute little guy on it to convince you to use it. That hardware, in case you missed it, is called Muse Charm , and it is, by CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s own description, “a joyful little device for talking to your Muse that fits on your keychain.” Despite how bad Meta seemingly wants you to use Muse, though, it may not wind up leading with a price that screams “buy me.” According to a report from The Information , Meta is targeting a $300 price tag for the Muse Charm, which is (in this economy and most others) a sizeable amount of money. Back in the day—just a couple of years ago, really—$300 used to get you a whole Xbox , though the RAM shortage has made those times feel like a dream you were sad to wake up from. The waking reality (possibly a nightmare) is $300 AI keychains, but don’t worry, Meta reportedly plans to sweeten that deal with free 5G data plans that would “enable faster responses for Muse.” That free ride, though, would last up to a year, after which I assume you’d have to pay a monthly sum of money to do something that you could just absolutely do on your phone instead. While some of you may be reading this and thinking, “Wow, Muse Charm sounds like a bad deal,” I can almost assure you Meta doth protest. The proof is in the pudding, or lack thereof in this case. According to The Information, Meta delayed its long-rumored plans to release a smartwatch so that it could focus on Muse Charm. If you were waiting for a Meta-made alternative to the Apple Watch, that stinks. But if you were like most people and frightened by the idea of what gross data-craven malfeasance Meta would get into with your most precious health data, then I guess Muse Charm is actually a minor win. Despite having an alleged price, the official details of what Muse Charm really does are scant. It has a small screen, microphones, and you can wear it around your neck like an immunity necklace if you were a participant in Survivor: Clanker Island. More details should be coming soon. Meta initially said that it was targeting a release around the holidays, so I guess you should start saving up to gift this expensive little charm to the favorite AI builder in your life. sources.title: Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
passages: Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information.
Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm.
Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

extraction.body: Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but he didn’t provide a price at the time. When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had “packed the whole Muse experience,” including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app. The Information reports that the Muse Charm will come with a free 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon. Spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote to The Information that “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” When reached for comment by The Verge, Yee provided the same statement. The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door. Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm. Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

sources.title: Meta's Muse Charm AI Keychain Reportedly Targets $300 Price Tag - BigGo Finance
passages: Meta is reportedly preparing to sell its upcoming AI keychain, the Muse Charm, for around $300, a price that would place the pocket-sized gadget well above several competing AI wearables already on the market.

A keychain-sized accessory priced near an entry-level game console or a mid-range smartwatch will be judged against devices that do far more, and the company will need the Muse experience to feel indispensable rather than novel.
The bundled connectivity suggests Meta intends to treat the charm as a subscription-adjacent product, with recurring revenue possibly arriving after the first year.
The device is designed to give Meta's software a physical form that users can carry in a pocket or wear around the neck.
It features a small screen and microphones, and lets users talk to Muse, ask questions and issue commands.
CEO Mark Zuckerberg has described it as "a joyful little device for talking to your Muse that fits on your keychain."
Note: Muse Charm pricing is reported and has not been confirmed by Meta.
The figure was reported by The Information, which said the company is aiming for that price point for the Tamagotchi-like device teased at Meta's Connect event earlier this year.
When asked about the report, a Meta spokesperson did not dispute the number, saying only: "We're charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we'll have more to share soon."
Meta has built a relatively successful consumer AI franchise around Muse and a range of cartoon-like avatars that give the assistant more personality.
The charm is its attempt to extend that software into hardware, a segment that has yet to produce a mainstream hit.
Humane's AI Pin became the most visible cautionary example, drawing poor reviews and weak sales.
Once added, BigGo Finance appears first in Google Search Top Stories, so you get the broadest, most up-to-the-minute, and most comprehensive global financial news first.
Official details on the product's full capabilities remain thin.
Meta initially said it was targeting a release around the holidays.
For investors, the launch is a small but telling test of whether Meta can convert its AI software lead into a hardware business.
If Meta can sell a $300 AI companion in volume, it would validate premium pricing for the category and pressure rivals to add features rather than cut prices.
If it cannot, the device risks becoming another example of AI hardware that generates headlines but not sustained demand.

Meta wants you to use Muse so bad, in fact, that it’s making hardware with a cute little guy on it to convince you to use it. That hardware, in case you missed it, is called Muse Charm , and it is, by CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s own description, “a joyful little device for talking to your Muse that fits on your keychain.” Despite how bad Meta seemingly wants you to use Muse, though, it may not wind up leading with a price that screams “buy me.” According to a report from The Information , Meta is targeting a $300 price tag for the Muse Charm, which is (in this economy and most others) a sizeable amount of money. Back in the day—just a couple of years ago, really—$300 used to get you a whole Xbox , though the RAM shortage has made those times feel like a dream you were sad to wake up from. The waking reality (possibly a nightmare) is $300 AI keychains, but don’t worry, Meta reportedly plans to sweeten that deal with free 5G data plans that would “enable faster responses for Muse.” That free ride, though, would last up to a year, after which I assume you’d have to pay a monthly sum of money to do something that you could just absolutely do on your phone instead. While some of you may be reading this and thinking, “Wow, Muse Charm sounds like a bad deal,” I can almost assure you Meta doth protest. The proof is in the pudding, or lack thereof in this case. According to The Information, Meta delayed its long-rumored plans to release a smartwatch so that it could focus on Muse Charm. If you were waiting for a Meta-made alternative to the Apple Watch, that stinks. But if you were like most people and frightened by the idea of what gross data-craven malfeasance Meta would get into with your most precious health data, then I guess Muse Charm is actually a minor win. Despite having an alleged price, the official details of what Muse Charm really does are scant. It has a small screen, microphones, and you can wear it around your neck like an immunity necklace if you were a participant in Survivor: Clanker Island. More details should be coming soon. Meta initially said that it was targeting a release around the holidays, so I guess you should start saving up to gift this expensive little charm to the favorite AI builder in your life. extraction.body: Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but he didn’t provide a price at the time. When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had “packed the whole Muse experience,” including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app. The Information reports that the Muse Charm will come with a free 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon. Spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote to The Information that “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” When reached for comment by The Verge, Yee provided the same statement. The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door. Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm. Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

CEO Mark Zuckerberg has described it as "a joyful little device for talking to your Muse that fits on your keychain." Official details on the product's full capabilities remain thin. Meta initially said it was targeting a release around the holidays. The reported price sits at the high end of a young and uneven category. Friend, a startup whose device lets users text and talk to an AI persona, sells its wearable for $250. The charm is its attempt to extend that software into hardware, a segment that has yet to produce a mainstream hit. Humane's AI Pin became the most visible cautionary example, drawing poor reviews and weak sales. For Meta, the $300 figure carries risk. A keychain-sized accessory priced near an entry-level game console or a mid-range smartwatch will be judged against devices that do far more, and the company will need the Muse experience to feel indispensable rather than novel. The bundled connectivity suggests Meta intends to treat the charm as a subscription-adjacent product, with recurring revenue possibly arriving after the first year. For investors, the launch is a small but telling test of whether Meta can convert its AI software lead into a hardware business. The company has not disclosed unit targets or revenue expectations, and the lack of confirmed specifications leaves open how much of the device's processing happens on board versus in the cloud, a factor that shapes both cost and the value of the free data plan. Competitors are watching closely. If Meta can sell a $300 AI companion in volume, it would validate premium pricing for the category and pressure rivals to add features rather than cut prices. extraction.body: CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years. Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation. China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns. Just a week ago it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. A lot has happened in the last few days, but how did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements. Megaspeed is the datacenter firm at the center of the spy allegations. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd . At this time, Megaspeed was controlled by a firm called Huang Le Ltd, an entity affiliated with Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg. Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry. Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips. Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered . The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband , Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal. The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times . The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Ali Baba. The commerce department begins investigating whether Megaspeed is diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, according to the New York Times. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips. Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office. The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after. The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan. The New York Times also reportes that Alice Huang visited the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, two months earlier. The New York Times reports in October 2025 that intelligence officials told Trump that the two had a relationship and alleged that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Trump chose not to take action, according to the Times report. Trump has since said at a White House press conference that he didn’t remember being briefed on this. Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second most powerful chips to China. A portion of the sales would go to the US government. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The memo warns that Jensen Huang has become close to an alleged Chinese spy. Trump still invites Huang on his trip to China, saying in a social media post that he is honored to have “the Great Jensen Huang” on the trip. At the time, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo says Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang is nothing out of the ordinary. In a letter to employees, Huang says that he had an extramarital affair, apologizes to his family and reaffirms his commitment to the company. The Nvidia board says it is investigating the relationship but has no reason to believe national security secrets or company secrets were divulged. “The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” members of the Board say in a statement. Silicon Valley leaders rally behind him , and at the time it appears that Huang might hang on to his job, despite his image being tarnished . At a press conference , Trump says the FBI is investigating Jensen Huang but adds that he thinks Huang will be “in good shape”. “And I asked him about that, and he … said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” the president says at a press conference. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’” Retail investor Mark Kistenmacher files a lawsuit accusing the company of misleading investors over Huang’s affair, claiming that Nvidia did not disclose the situation and raised national security concerns that could threaten the company’s business prospects. The New York Times reports that Huang also allegedly had an affair with the company’s vice-president of healthcare. At this point things are looking precarious for Jensen Huang, and then the Wall Street Journal reports that the Nvidia board is preparing to oust the CEO. Huang steps down, ending his 33-year tenure leading the company he co-founded in 1993. The board starts a search for the company’s next CEO while the company’s chief finance officer, Colette Kress, serves as interim CEO. Meanwhile, shares in the company continue to plummet.

extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations. The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory. “We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress said. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones affirmed that the company is not considering reinstating Huang. Kress also said that Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. Jensen Huang posted his first public statement since he admitted to having an extramarital affair more than a week earlier. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote. Many of Huang’s colleagues in the tech industry, including Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey , and Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan, have called for his return. Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an… More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is at the centre of a controversy that has moved well beyond his personal life. What began as reports of his close relationship with Alice Huang, suspected of spying for China, has developed into a wider national security and corporate governance issue. The controversy has drawn attention from US lawmakers, prompted an independent investigation by Nvidia's board and reportedly raised questions about Huang's future at the company. Here is how the events unfolded, from the initial investigations into a Singapore-based business to the latest developments surrounding the Nvidia chief. October 2025: Chip smuggling investigation The controversy has its roots in investigations into Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company and Nvidia customer. In October 2025, authorities in the US and Singapore began investigating the company over suspicions that it was helping Chinese businesses obtain Nvidia chips despite American export restrictions. According to reports, Megaspeed had been renting computing capacity to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other companies. Concerns grew after a US Commerce Department official visiting one of its data centres in Malaysia in 2024 reportedly discovered Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes, raising questions about whether the hardware was being shipped elsewhere rather than deployed for cloud computing. Huang had also been seen socialising with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang in Taiwan as early as 2024. Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is not related to the Nvidia CEO. 2025: Trump reportedly briefed on Huang's relationship US President Donald Trump was reportedly briefed towards the end of 2025 about intelligence findings concerning Alice Huang and her relationship with the Nvidia chief. However, the president did not take action following the briefing, according to the New York Times. Huang has been an ally of Trump and has repeatedly argued that the US government should allow Nvidia to expand its business in China. May 2026: Secret memo raises concerns about suspected Chinese spy The matter took another turn in spring 2026 when a confidential memo circulated among Trump administration officials. The document reportedly identified Alice Huang as a suspected Chinese intelligence operative working for China's Ministry of State Security. According to reports, Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the preparation of the memo. It warned policymakers about her alleged relationship with Huang and the potential implications for American national security. October 29, 2026: Huang's relationship with Alice Huang becomes public The controversy became public when the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, who was already under investigation by American authorities. Nvidia pushed back against suggestions that their interactions were unusual. Company spokesperson John Rizzo said meetings with customers were part of Huang's responsibilities as chief executive, adding that he interacted with thousands of customer executives every year. He also said Nvidia would expect the US government to inform the company if it believed someone posed a threat to American industry. November 5, 2026: Republican lawmakers seek answers from Huang Three Republican committee chairmen asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing with members of their committees. The lawmakers included John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. Their letter highlighted concerns about China's access to sensitive American technology and information. They said Congress needed to establish whether US national security had been compromised through potential Chinese infiltration. November 8, 2026: Huang apologises for affair as Nvidia, FDA launches investigation Huang addressed the controversy directly in a letter to Nvidia employees, admitting that he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologising to his family and colleagues. Although he did not identify Alice Huang by name, he acknowledged the national security concerns raised in media reports. Huang also confirmed that Nvidia's board had initiated an independent investigation, pledging to cooperate fully and reiterating his commitment to protecting the company and American national security. The admission had an immediate impact on investor sentiment, with Nvidia shares falling more than 5 per cent the following day. US President Donald Trump also weighed in on the controversy on November 8. Despite acknowledging that he did not know all the details, Trump described Huang as a 'fine person' and said he believed the Nvidia chief should remain in charge of the company. November 9-10, 2026: More about Alice Huang's business network Further reporting shed light on the business connections between Alice Huang, her family and Nvidia's chip supply chain. According to reports, Alice Huang and her family had established a network of businesses across China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia processors. One of these was Shanghai Century Litong, a Chinese company founded in 2023 that reportedly became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips. The Information reported that the company had facilitated purchases worth $7.5 billion, including chips restricted under US export controls. Separately, Bloomberg reported that Nvidia's head lawyer, Tim Teter, had intervened during a 2025 US government investigation into suspected chip smuggling involving Megaspeed.

extraction.body: CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years. Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation. China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns. Just a week ago it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. A lot has happened in the last few days, but how did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements. Megaspeed is the datacenter firm at the center of the spy allegations. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd . At this time, Megaspeed was controlled by a firm called Huang Le Ltd, an entity affiliated with Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg. Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry. Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips. Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered . The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband , Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal. The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times . The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Ali Baba. The commerce department begins investigating whether Megaspeed is diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, according to the New York Times. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips. Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office. The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after. The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan. The New York Times also reportes that Alice Huang visited the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, two months earlier. The New York Times reports in October 2025 that intelligence officials told Trump that the two had a relationship and alleged that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Trump chose not to take action, according to the Times report. Trump has since said at a White House press conference that he didn’t remember being briefed on this. Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second most powerful chips to China. A portion of the sales would go to the US government. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The memo warns that Jensen Huang has become close to an alleged Chinese spy. Trump still invites Huang on his trip to China, saying in a social media post that he is honored to have “the Great Jensen Huang” on the trip. At the time, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo says Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang is nothing out of the ordinary. In a letter to employees, Huang says that he had an extramarital affair, apologizes to his family and reaffirms his commitment to the company. The Nvidia board says it is investigating the relationship but has no reason to believe national security secrets or company secrets were divulged. “The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” members of the Board say in a statement. Silicon Valley leaders rally behind him , and at the time it appears that Huang might hang on to his job, despite his image being tarnished . Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years.

Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation.

China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns.

Just a week ago it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive.

Megaspeed is the datacenter firm at the center of the spy allegations. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd . Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry.
Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips.

Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered . The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband , Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times . The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Ali Baba.

The commerce department begins investigating whether Megaspeed is diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, according to the New York Times. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips.
Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office.
The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after.
The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan. The New York Times also reportes that Alice Huang visited the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, two months earlier.

extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations. The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory. “We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress said. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones affirmed that the company is not considering reinstating Huang. Kress also said that Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. Jensen Huang posted his first public statement since he admitted to having an extramarital affair more than a week earlier. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote. Many of Huang’s colleagues in the tech industry, including Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey , and Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan, have called for his return. Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an… More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.” Get an Early Peek at the Next TechCrunch Disrupt Disrupt, Startup Battlefield, and more will return next year, and you can be at the front of the line. extraction.body: Chinese artificial intelligence developer Moonshot AI has walked away from a $150 million arrangement to run Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) hardware inside Indonesian data centers, abandoning the plan within days of a new American rule aimed at shutting down offshore renting of restricted chips. The cancellation, first reported in the crypto and AI trade press, lands as Washington moves to treat remote access to advanced processors the same way it treats physical shipments. Moonshot, the Beijing-based builder of the Kimi model family, is said to be scouting alternatives, including preliminary discussions with data center operators in Europe. At the center of the shift is an interim final rule issued Nov. 16 by the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security. The measure, drafted by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, requires a license before advanced chips can be exported, re-exported or transferred within a country to any data center that supplies more than 12 million units of total processing performance to customers headquartered in China or other restricted jurisdictions, a group that also covers Russia, Iran, North Korea and Macau. That threshold works out to roughly 750 to 760 top-end Nvidia H100 or H200 accelerators, according to estimates from the Center for a New American Security, a Washington think tank. For scale, that is about a third of the computing power DeepSeek is reported to have used to train its V3 model. The rule also imposes licensing requirements on advanced semiconductor shipments to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which U.S. officials say carry an elevated risk of diversion. Suppliers can still ship to American-headquartered customers in those five countries without a license, provided they file a monthly report with the government. Separately, the package formally rescinds the Biden administration's AI Diffusion Rule, which had sorted countries into tiers to determine chip access. For data centers already serving Chinese customers above the threshold, the rule provides a 90-day window to apply for a license before access is cut off. The version first posted by the agency still carried a placeholder for its effective date, leaving the start of that countdown unclear. Moonshot had good reason to keep hunting for capacity. Its Kimi K3, released in July, carries 2.8 trillion parameters and came close to matching leading systems from Anthropic and OpenAI on standard benchmarks. Demand ran so hot within two days of launch that the company nearly exhausted its chips and stopped accepting new sign-ups. The White House said in July that Moonshot had accessed Nvidia's Blackwell processors through a Thai data center around the time Kimi K3 debuted. Beijing reacted sharply. China's commerce ministry said it firmly opposes the rule and would take countermeasures if Washington presses ahead, while urging a return to consultation. The timing carries diplomatic weight: the measure landed as President Donald Trump departed for an Asia trip that includes a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The rule's reach is not absolute. Analysts note that a developer could stay under the processing-performance ceiling by spreading a workload across multiple providers. Enforcement also hinges on exporters and data center operators establishing who their customers actually are; a facility that declines to confirm the identity of its users is itself treated as a red flag. The Commerce Secretary retains authority to add more countries to the licensing list, a standing source of uncertainty for operators in unaffected markets. Some data center operators have reportedly begun asking Chinese clients such as Moonshot for 30% to 50% more cash upfront to insulate themselves against exactly this kind of regulatory shock. The new rule is the latest step in a years-long tightening of the U.S. export control architecture. Chinese firms are barred from legally importing Nvidia's most capable chips, so many have instead paid by the hour for compute housed in Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and elsewhere. That rental route sat outside the letter of U.S. export law until now. Enforcement officials began studying how to close the gap in August, and the Center for a New American Security estimates remote access will account for roughly 23% of China's AI chip supply by the end of 2026. The package also narrows the presumption rules governing advanced logic chips made at overseas foundries and assembly plants, shifting the burden of proof onto manufacturers to show a chip is not destined for a restricted end user. Chip designers in restricted regions would need to secure a place on a BIS-approved designer list to overcome that presumption. Market reaction was swift. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 5.3% as the measure circulated. The stock sits at the center of the AI trade, and the rule arrived in a crowded week for the chipmaker: interim CEO Colette Kress said the company will stop shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China after booking $2.4 billion from them in the quarter, and guidance now assumes no data center compute revenue from the country at all. Third-quarter revenue roughly doubled from a year earlier to $115.8 billion, with guidance of about $130 billion for the current period. Note: Chip-count equivalents and the processing-performance threshold come from Center for a New American Security estimates; Nvidia figures are from the company's quarterly results. The immediate read for investors is that the offshore rental channel, one of the last open paths to American-designed compute for Chinese AI developers, is narrowing fast. Southeast Asia has become a data center hub largely on the back of demand from Chinese firms, and the five-country licensing list targets that buildout directly. Nvidia's own numbers suggest the company can keep posting records while treating China as absent from its forecast, a signal of how much of the AI spending cycle now runs without Beijing. Whether the closure holds will depend on how forcefully the rule is enforced, how China responds, and whether the next workaround is already under construction. The cancellation came days after the U.S. Commerce Department issued a new rule to stop Chinese firms from renting banned chips abroad. Moonshot is reportedly still looking for other options, including talks with data center operators in Europe. Moonshot has canceled its $150 million deal to use Nvidia chips through data centers in Indonesia due to a new U.S. rule. Chinese companies cannot legally import Nvidia’s most powerful chips and so instead of buying the chips, they pay by the hour to use them in data centers in countries like Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia. Until now, this renting route fell outside U.S. export law. In August, U.S. enforcement officials reportedly began studying how to close this gap. One estimate cited by the Center for a New American Security (CNAS), a think tank in the United States, says remote access will make up about 23% of China’s access to AI chips by the end of 2026. On November 16, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a new rule . It was reportedly written at the request of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council. Under the rule, companies need a license to ship advanced chips to any data center that gives more than 12 million units of “total processing performance” to customers based in China or other restricted countries. Michelle Nie Duncan, an analyst at CNAS, wrote that this is about 760 Nvidia H100 chips. That is roughly one third of the computing power DeepSeek is reported to have used to train its V3 model. The rule also adds a license requirement for advanced chip shipments to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the U.S. government says carry a higher-than-normal risk of chips being diverted. Companies can ship these chips to US-based customers in those five countries without a license, but only if they send the government a report every month. The new rule also scraps the Biden administration’s AI Diffusion Rule that ranked countries by tier to decide who could buy chips. In July, the White House said Moonshot had used Nvidia’s Blackwell chips through a data center in Thailand. This was around the time it launched its Kimi K3 model. Earlier this month, Moonshot was reported to be talking to data center operators in Europe about renting Blackwell chips. One offer involved groups of 8,000 or more chips. Data centers that already serve Chinese customers get 90 days to apply for a license under the new rule before they lose access. The document first posted by BIS still listed its effective date as a placeholder, so it is currently unclear when the 90-day countdown will begin. The size limit for the rule also leaves room for Chinese AI firms to work around it. CNAS noted that a developer could stay under the limit by splitting a job across several providers. Another gap in the rule is that it depends on exporters and data centers finding out who their customers are, and if a data center won’t confirm who is using its chips, then that counts as a red flag. extraction.body: Chinese artificial intelligence developer Moonshot AI has walked away from a $150 million arrangement to run Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) hardware inside Indonesian data centers, abandoning the plan within days of a new American rule aimed at shutting down offshore renting of restricted chips. The cancellation, first reported in the crypto and AI trade press, lands as Washington moves to treat remote access to advanced processors the same way it treats physical shipments. Moonshot, the Beijing-based builder of the Kimi model family, is said to be scouting alternatives, including preliminary discussions with data center operators in Europe. At the center of the shift is an interim final rule issued Nov. 16 by the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security. The measure, drafted by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, requires a license before advanced chips can be exported, re-exported or transferred within a country to any data center that supplies more than 12 million units of total processing performance to customers headquartered in China or other restricted jurisdictions, a group that also covers Russia, Iran, North Korea and Macau. That threshold works out to roughly 750 to 760 top-end Nvidia H100 or H200 accelerators, according to estimates from the Center for a New American Security, a Washington think tank. For scale, that is about a third of the computing power DeepSeek is reported to have used to train its V3 model. The rule also imposes licensing requirements on advanced semiconductor shipments to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which U.S. officials say carry an elevated risk of diversion. Suppliers can still ship to American-headquartered customers in those five countries without a license, provided they file a monthly report with the government. Separately, the package formally rescinds the Biden administration's AI Diffusion Rule, which had sorted countries into tiers to determine chip access. For data centers already serving Chinese customers above the threshold, the rule provides a 90-day window to apply for a license before access is cut off. The version first posted by the agency still carried a placeholder for its effective date, leaving the start of that countdown unclear. Moonshot had good reason to keep hunting for capacity. Its Kimi K3, released in July, carries 2.8 trillion parameters and came close to matching leading systems from Anthropic and OpenAI on standard benchmarks. Demand ran so hot within two days of launch that the company nearly exhausted its chips and stopped accepting new sign-ups. The White House said in July that Moonshot had accessed Nvidia's Blackwell processors through a Thai data center around the time Kimi K3 debuted. Beijing reacted sharply. China's commerce ministry said it firmly opposes the rule and would take countermeasures if Washington presses ahead, while urging a return to consultation. The timing carries diplomatic weight: the measure landed as President Donald Trump departed for an Asia trip that includes a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The rule's reach is not absolute. Analysts note that a developer could stay under the processing-performance ceiling by spreading a workload across multiple providers. Enforcement also hinges on exporters and data center operators establishing who their customers actually are; a facility that declines to confirm the identity of its users is itself treated as a red flag. The Commerce Secretary retains authority to add more countries to the licensing list, a standing source of uncertainty for operators in unaffected markets. Some data center operators have reportedly begun asking Chinese clients such as Moonshot for 30% to 50% more cash upfront to insulate themselves against exactly this kind of regulatory shock. The new rule is the latest step in a years-long tightening of the U.S. export control architecture. Chinese firms are barred from legally importing Nvidia's most capable chips, so many have instead paid by the hour for compute housed in Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and elsewhere. That rental route sat outside the letter of U.S. export law until now. Enforcement officials began studying how to close the gap in August, and the Center for a New American Security estimates remote access will account for roughly 23% of China's AI chip supply by the end of 2026. The package also narrows the presumption rules governing advanced logic chips made at overseas foundries and assembly plants, shifting the burden of proof onto manufacturers to show a chip is not destined for a restricted end user. Chip designers in restricted regions would need to secure a place on a BIS-approved designer list to overcome that presumption. Market reaction was swift. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 5.3% as the measure circulated. The stock sits at the center of the AI trade, and the rule arrived in a crowded week for the chipmaker: interim CEO Colette Kress said the company will stop shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China after booking $2.4 billion from them in the quarter, and guidance now assumes no data center compute revenue from the country at all. Third-quarter revenue roughly doubled from a year earlier to $115.8 billion, with guidance of about $130 billion for the current period. Note: Chip-count equivalents and the processing-performance threshold come from Center for a New American Security estimates; Nvidia figures are from the company's quarterly results. The immediate read for investors is that the offshore rental channel, one of the last open paths to American-designed compute for Chinese AI developers, is narrowing fast. Southeast Asia has become a data center hub largely on the back of demand from Chinese firms, and the five-country licensing list targets that buildout directly. Nvidia's own numbers suggest the company can keep posting records while treating China as absent from its forecast, a signal of how much of the AI spending cycle now runs without Beijing. Whether the closure holds will depend on how forcefully the rule is enforced, how China responds, and whether the next workaround is already under construction. The cancellation came days after the U.S. Commerce Department issued a new rule to stop Chinese firms from renting banned chips abroad. Moonshot is reportedly still looking for other options, including talks with data center operators in Europe. Moonshot has canceled its $150 million deal to use Nvidia chips through data centers in Indonesia due to a new U.S. rule. Chinese companies cannot legally import Nvidia’s most powerful chips and so instead of buying the chips, they pay by the hour to use them in data centers in countries like Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia. Until now, this renting route fell outside U.S. export law. In August, U.S. enforcement officials reportedly began studying how to close this gap. One estimate cited by the Center for a New American Security (CNAS), a think tank in the United States, says remote access will make up about 23% of China’s access to AI chips by the end of 2026. On November 16, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a new rule . It was reportedly written at the request of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council. Under the rule, companies need a license to ship advanced chips to any data center that gives more than 12 million units of “total processing performance” to customers based in China or other restricted countries. Michelle Nie Duncan, an analyst at CNAS, wrote that this is about 760 Nvidia H100 chips. That is roughly one third of the computing power DeepSeek is reported to have used to train its V3 model. The rule also adds a license requirement for advanced chip shipments to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the U.S. government says carry a higher-than-normal risk of chips being diverted. Companies can ship these chips to US-based customers in those five countries without a license, but only if they send the government a report every month. The new rule also scraps the Biden administration’s AI Diffusion Rule that ranked countries by tier to decide who could buy chips. In July, the White House said Moonshot had used Nvidia’s Blackwell chips through a data center in Thailand. This was around the time it launched its Kimi K3 model. Earlier this month, Moonshot was reported to be talking to data center operators in Europe about renting Blackwell chips. One offer involved groups of 8,000 or more chips. Data centers that already serve Chinese customers get 90 days to apply for a license under the new rule before they lose access. The document first posted by BIS still listed its effective date as a placeholder, so it is currently unclear when the 90-day countdown will begin. The size limit for the rule also leaves room for Chinese AI firms to work around it. CNAS noted that a developer could stay under the limit by splitting a job across several providers. Another gap in the rule is that it depends on exporters and data centers finding out who their customers are, and if a data center won’t confirm who is using its chips, then that counts as a red flag. Moonshot has strong reasons to keep looking for chips. Its Kimi K3, which was released in July, is a model with 2.8 trillion parameters that nearly matched the top systems from Anthropic and OpenAI on benchmarks. Just two days after launch, the demand for Kimi K3 was so high that Moonshot nearly ran out of chips and had to stop accepting new sign-ups. Some data center operators have also reportedly asked Chinese customers like Moonshot to pay 30% to 50% more upfront, to protect themselves against rules like this one. Issued by BIS on November 16, it requires a license to supply covered chips to any data center serving Chinese or other restricted customers above 12 million TPP (about 760 H100 chips), and it adds export-license requirements for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. China cannot legally import Nvidia's top processors, but renting access to them in third-country data centers has sat outside US export controls, a loophole projected to account for about 23% of China's AI chip access by the end of 2026. The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public. "Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday. Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California. extraction.body: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has served Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) with an investigative subpoena as part of a probe into whether its advanced semiconductors reached China in violation of U.S. export controls, his office said Thursday. The inquiry is tied to the widening fallout from the departure of former chief executive Jensen Huang, who stepped down last week after acknowledging an extramarital affair. Bonta said the company's conduct and that of its former leader have raised serious questions. "The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," Bonta said in a statement. "My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law." The attorney general framed the matter as a test of basic corporate securities obligations. "Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation, but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," he said. At the center of the scrutiny is Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data company that has been under investigation over suspicions it diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, has been identified by U.S. intelligence officials as suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services, according to the Wall Street Journal. Nvidia has previously denied that Jensen Huang had an unusual relationship with her. Separately, the SEC has opened a civil investigation into whether Nvidia's investor disclosures accurately described its business, the Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The precise focus of that probe remains unclear. The company also drew congressional attention and questions from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who asked the board and outside counsel to answer within 10 days whether questionable sales were used to inflate earnings. Huang has acknowledged falling short of company expectations, saying in a statement released Tuesday: "I own my mistakes completely." The disclosure questions extend to how Nvidia reports overseas revenue. The chipmaker revised its international sales disclosures last year and removed a separate breakdown of sales to Singapore, where Megaspeed was headquartered. Several businesses in Southeast Asia used Nvidia chips to build AI data centers, and authorities suspect some of that hardware was routed to China. Investors have punished the stock. Nvidia shares are down 22% over the nine trading days since Huang admitted the affair, putting the stock on course for a seventh consecutive weekly decline and a 38% loss over that span, according to CNBC. The regulatory pressure adds a new legal front for the world's most valuable chipmaker, which is already navigating export restrictions that limit what it can sell in China. A state securities investigation carries potential civil penalties, while an SEC probe can lead to enforcement action or disclosure requirements. For investors, the overlapping inquiries raise the risk of restated disclosures and prolonged uncertainty over the company's China exposure, a market that has been central to its growth story. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. (NVDA) with an investigative subpoena as part of a probe into whether its advanced semiconductors reached China in violation of U.S. export controls, his office said Thursday. The inquiry is tied to the widening fallout from the departure of former chief executive Jensen Huang, who stepped down last week after acknowledging an extramarital affair. Bonta said the company's conduct and that of its former leader have raised serious questions. "The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," Bonta said in a statement. "My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law." The attorney general framed the matter as a test of basic corporate securities obligations. "Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation, but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," he said. At the center of the scrutiny is Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data company that has been under investigation over suspicions it diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, has been identified by U.S. intelligence officials as suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services, according to the Wall Street Journal. Nvidia has previously denied that Jensen Huang had an unusual relationship with her. Separately, the SEC has opened a civil investigation into whether Nvidia's investor disclosures accurately described its business, the Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The precise focus of that probe remains unclear. The company also drew congressional attention and questions from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who asked the board and outside counsel to answer within 10 days whether questionable sales were used to inflate earnings. Huang has acknowledged falling short of company expectations, saying in a statement released Tuesday: "I own my mistakes completely." The disclosure questions extend to how Nvidia reports overseas revenue. The chipmaker revised its international sales disclosures last year and removed a separate breakdown of sales to Singapore, where Megaspeed was headquartered. Several businesses in Southeast Asia used Nvidia chips to build AI data centers, and authorities suspect some of that hardware was routed to China. Investors have punished the stock. Nvidia shares are down 22% over the nine trading days since Huang admitted the affair, putting the stock on course for a seventh consecutive weekly decline and a 38% loss over that span, according to CNBC. The regulatory pressure adds a new legal front for the world's most valuable chipmaker, which is already navigating export restrictions that limit what it can sell in China. A state securities investigation carries potential civil penalties, while an SEC probe can lead to enforcement action or disclosure requirements. For investors, the overlapping inquiries raise the risk of restated disclosures and prolonged uncertainty over the company's China exposure, a market that has been central to its growth story. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. coreStoryFacts.text: The Donald Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said on Thursday.

"The fact that over 30% of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses,” said Chris McGuire, a former U.S. official and expert on the U.S.-China technology battle.
Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the documents showed.
The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the administration of U.S.

President Donald Trump faces heightened scrutiny ⁠following news about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China.
AMD said it "complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations."

In testimony before ⁠the committee in July, Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler said shipments had begun but there had been 'very few.' Several major Chinese internet companies had each obtained about 10,000 H200 chips, Reuters has since reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

WASHINGTON - The Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said on Thursday.

“The fact that over 30% of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses,” said Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle.
Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the documents showed.
Former President Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China’s military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence.

The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the administration of President Donald Trump faces heightened scrutiny following news about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China.

In testimony before the committee in July, Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler said shipments had begun but there had been “very few.” Several major Chinese internet companies had each obtained about 10,000 H200 chips, Reuters has since reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

“The fact that over 30 percent of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses,” said Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle.

The administration of United States President Donald Trump approved exports of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee has said.
Companies had sought permission to ship 3.4 million of them to China during the period, committee documents show.
It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of the chips, which included Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent MI325X.
Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were “subject to strict conditions and limited volumes”.
It added that “despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China”.
The US House Foreign Committee released the chip export licensing data amid Nvidia’s ex-CEO’s affair with alleged Chinese spy.
