extraction.body: House committee data show the Donald Trump administration authorized major Nvidia and AMD chip sales to Chinese firms, including companies flagged for military ties. The Donald Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said on Thursday. The approvals for 879,000 chip shipments by the Commerce Department included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD, all on the Pentagon's list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies, the committee noted. The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump faces heightened scrutiny ⁠following news about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China. Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the documents showed. It ⁠was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of chips, which included Nvidia's H200 and AMD's equivalent MI325X. News surrounding Huang has turned a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats. "The fact that over 30% of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses,” said Chris McGuire, a former U.S. official and expert on the U.S.-China technology battle. Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were "subject to strict conditions and limited volumes." It added that "despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped ⁠shipping H200s to China." AMD said it "complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations." Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, BYD, the Commerce Department and the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Former President Joe Biden ⁠had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that ⁠they would supercharge China's military and erode the U.S. lead in AI. But Trump in December gave the green light for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the U.S. political spectrum. Despite the approvals, questions swirled as to whether the AI chips were actually reaching Chinese shores. In May, Reuters reported that the United States had cleared ⁠about 10 companies to buy the H200, but that no deliveries had ⁠taken place. In testimony before ⁠the committee in July, Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler said shipments had begun but there had been 'very few.' Several major Chinese internet companies had each obtained about 10,000 H200 chips, Reuters has since reported, citing people familiar with the matter. "This is the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act," committee Chair Brian Mast, a Republican from Florida, said upon releasing the data, referring to 2018 legislation that expanded Commerce's authority to restrict the export of sensitive technologies for national security reasons. U.S. President Donald Trump said he and Chinese President Xi Jinping want to coordinate on reasonable AI regulations as the two countries compete for technological leadership. Banks are cutting their exposure through deals with insurers as the issuance of asset-backed securities tumbles. Spending at Korea’s major chains has more than doubled as K-content and social media turn everyday shopping into a tourist activity. Korea’s top health and beauty retailer is using AI, data and unified logistics to connect stores, apps and global expansion.

Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were “subject to strict conditions and limited volumes.” It added that “despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China.” AMD said it “complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations.” Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, BYD, the Commerce Department and the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment. passages: Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
Update 11/19/2026 12:05 PM PT: The article was updated to include Meta’s comment.

In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.

sources.title: Meta Employees Raise Privacy Concerns Over Muse AI Mixing Up Accounts: 5 outlets compared - NewsCord
passages: Meta launched its Muse AI agent in September 2026 with a promise that it was built from the ground up for privacy and security, but Reuters reviewed internal communications showing employees raising “significant concerns” about Muse’s handling of private data.

Reuters reported that internal posts described incidents where Muse appeared to be mixing up conversations between different user accounts, and employees flagged safety issues “as recently as launch week” while Meta proceeded with the September 2026 US launch as scheduled.
Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests employees said they never made and bank account balances that did not belong to them.

Muse had already been downloaded by more than 10 million people and Meta expected it to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI, while La Nación described internal postings reviewed by Reuters as showing unsolicited actions including infiltrating encrypted personal messages and sending conversations that appeared destined for other people.

The Defense Watch said Reuters could not establish whether unfamiliar financial information represented actual exposure of another person’s data or information fabricated by the AI model, and the outlet described Meta’s position that many messages identified as possible account mix-ups were hallucinations and that some problems had already been addressed.
This article is an automated aggregation of coverage from news outlets.
Our editorials offer in-depth analysis curated by the NewsCord team.
5 outlets in this story. Read their headlines below .

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told TechCrunch that “employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public,” and Roberts described Reuters’ examples as “isolated incidents.” Ars Technica quoted a Meta staffer writing “Hmmm,” after Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden, and Ars Technica also quoted the staffer’s out-of-context output about a coffee table pickup that “doesn’t seem to be yours.”
Meta Muse reportedly mixes conversations from different accounts, exposing private data.
Internal testing flagged Muse accessing encrypted private messages users did not expect.

Claroc discovered that Muse’s chat-sharing feature exposed shared conversations through publicly searchable DNS records, and Claroc found that users who shared a conversation did not realize the resulting links were discoverable by anyone with the right DNS query.
Muse accessed private Signal messages on the device where it was installed, made possible by the broad Android notification permissions the app requests.

Each Muse agent runs in its own cloud virtual machine, gated by a separate security process called Sentinel.Is Meta Muse a Security Liability?Based on the Reuters investigation, Claroc's research, and the Ars Technica reporting on internal Meta communications, Muse had experienced multiple distinct security and privacy failures by November 2026, two months after its US launch.The failures range from the DNS-accessible shared chat links, which exposed conversations that users believed were private, to internal testing that showed Muse reading Signal messages without direct user instruction, to employees reporting cross-account data confusion during testing.

Meta did not dispute that the internal posts existed.Separately, security firm Claroc discovered that the chat-sharing feature in Muse exposed shared conversations through publicly searchable DNS records.

During controlled tests conducted by Reuters, Muse accessed private Signal messages on the device where it was installed, made possible by the broad Android notification permissions the app requests.Muse also sent employees unsolicited bank balance figures from an unidentified source during testing, raising concerns about where the financial data was originating from and how the agent was processing information it had not been directly prompted to retrieve.Employees also raised concerns about a human concierge feature that Meta had been developing alongside Muse.

Meta is one of the most widely used technology companies in the world, with billions of users across its apps, and it generates revenue primarily through advertising across its social media platforms.What Is Meta Muse?Meta Muse is an AI agent developed by Meta and launched for US users in September 2026.

Founded by Mark Zuckerberg in 2004 as Facebook, the company rebranded as Meta in 2021 to reflect its focus on the development of the metaverse and augmented reality hardware through its Quest VR headset line. Meta is one of the most widely used technology companies in the world, with billions of users across its apps, and it generates revenue primarily through advertising across its social media platforms.What Is Meta Muse?Meta Muse is an AI agent developed by Meta and launched for US users in September 2026. coreStoryFacts.text: Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
Update 11/19/2026 12:05 PM PT: The article was updated to include Meta’s comment.

Reuters reported that internal posts described incidents where Muse appeared to be mixing up conversations between different user accounts, and employees flagged safety issues “as recently as launch week” while Meta proceeded with the September 2026 US launch as scheduled.

Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests employees said they never made and bank account balances that did not belong to them. Ars Technica reported that internal chats showed staffers warning Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, and Ars Technica quoted a staffer writing “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”

Reuters reported that Claroc confirmed it had no evidence that anyone had misused the exposed chats before the issue was identified, and Claroc said Meta temporarily disabled the sharing feature while it investigated the problem. Meta restored the feature with a fix in place, and Claroc confirmed that the previously accessible links were no longer reachable.

passages: Meta launched its Muse AI agent with a promise that it was built from the ground up for privacy and security.A recent investigation and several reports reveal that the people testing the product internally were raising serious doubts about whether that promise was being met before and even after the product shipped.Meta Employees Expose Muse AI Privacy ConcernsReuters reviewed internal communications at Meta that showed employees raising significant concerns about Muse's handling of private data, including incidents where the AI agent appeared to be mixing up conversations between different user accounts.

Each Muse agent runs in its own cloud virtual machine, gated by a separate security process called Sentinel.Is Meta Muse a Security Liability?Based on the Reuters investigation, Claroc's research, and the Ars Technica reporting on internal Meta communications, Muse had experienced multiple distinct security and privacy failures by November 2026, two months after its US launch.The failures range from the DNS-accessible shared chat links, which exposed conversations that users believed were private, to internal testing that showed Muse reading Signal messages without direct user instruction, to employees reporting cross-account data confusion during testing.

Meta did not dispute that the internal posts existed.Separately, security firm Claroc discovered that the chat-sharing feature in Muse exposed shared conversations through publicly searchable DNS records.

Those internal posts revealed a pattern of safety issues that employees believed could expose private data, with some describing failure modes that made the product unreliable in real-world conditions.Employees testing Muse as recently as launch week flagged these concerns through internal channels, yet Meta proceeded with the September 2026 US launch as scheduled.

During controlled tests conducted by Reuters, Muse accessed private Signal messages on the device where it was installed, made possible by the broad Android notification permissions the app requests.Muse also sent employees unsolicited bank balance figures from an unidentified source during testing, raising concerns about where the financial data was originating from and how the agent was processing information it had not been directly prompted to retrieve.Employees also raised concerns about a human concierge feature that Meta had been developing alongside Muse.

Security researchers needed a single DNS query to surface thousands of previously shared chat links, all of which were accessible to anyone who found them, without any login requirement.The exposed conversations were created by users who had explicitly chosen to share them with specific recipients but did not expect that those links would be discoverable by third parties.

The internal chats reviewed by Ars Technica showed employees describing Muse behavior that they found alarming, and that conflicted directly with how the product had been marketed to the public.Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat Is Meta?Meta Platforms, Inc. is an American technology company headquartered in Menlo Park, California, and is the parent company of Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Threads, as well as the developer of Meta AI, Muse, and the company's portfolio of AI products.

The sharing feature vulnerability was identified, reported to Meta through a bug bounty program, and patched.For users who want to minimize risk while using Muse, security researchers and IT experts recommend treating any AI agent with broad device permissions with caution, avoiding sharing conversations containing sensitive personal, financial, or business information through any AI tool's share feature, and monitoring the app's permission settings to understand what data Muse can access.

Meta is one of the most widely used technology companies in the world, with billions of users across its apps, and it generates revenue primarily through advertising across its social media platforms.What Is Meta Muse?Meta Muse is an AI agent developed by Meta and launched for US users in September 2026.

Organizations using Muse in business contexts should establish clear internal policies about which categories of information employees may submit to AI assistants and audit which tools are connected to business accounts.

The internal chats reviewed by Ars Technica showed employees describing Muse behavior that they found alarming, and that conflicted directly with how the product had been marketed to the public.Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat Is Meta?Meta Platforms, Inc. is an American technology company headquartered in Menlo Park, California, and is the parent company of Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Threads, as well as the developer of Meta AI, Muse, and the company's portfolio of AI products. Founded by Mark Zuckerberg in 2004 as Facebook, the company rebranded as Meta in 2021 to reflect its focus on the development of the metaverse and augmented reality hardware through its Quest VR headset line. Meta is one of the most widely used technology companies in the world, with billions of users across its apps, and it generates revenue primarily through advertising across its social media platforms.What Is Meta Muse?Meta Muse is an AI agent developed by Meta and launched for US users in September 2026. Zuckerberg described Muse at launch as a personal AI assistant built from the ground up for privacy and security. The agent is designed to autonomously manage tasks across a user's digital life, including reading and composing emails, managing calendar events, handling financial tasks through connected payment accounts, making phone calls on behalf of the user, browsing the internet, and acting on information drawn from connected apps and devices. Muse operates through broad device permissions that allow it to access notifications, messages, and other data from other apps installed on the same device in order to provide context-aware assistance. extraction.body: The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, there had been 3.4 million requested sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices . "Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents. The Commerce Department, AMD and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment. "The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks continued. The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest." The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including Bytedance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu . The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China. In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries. Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS — Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions. "Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting. Maginfra and New Matrix did not immediately reply to requests for comment. Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers." CNBC did not independently verify this information. Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance. Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify. Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China. Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third controls. The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release. This is breaking news. passages: The revelation that Commerce approved 879,000 AI chip sales to China has transformed what was already a crisis at Nvidia into a full-blown political reckoning for the entire semiconductor industry.

The Commerce Department signed off on selling more than 879,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, a number that's now driving urgent calls on Capitol Hill for a complete overhaul of America's semiconductor export regime.
It's a no-win situation for chipmakers: sell to China and face Congressional fury, or leave billions in revenue on the table to appease Washington.
Brian Mast dropped the bombshell figure during hearings this week, revealing an approval volume that far exceeds what most lawmakers believed was flowing to China under current restrictions.
Kress delivered better-than-expected earnings in her first quarterly report as interim CEO, but the China export controversy has overshadowed those results.
Nvidia just completed its fastest product ramp ever with the H200, shipping thousands of units weekly before the China halt kicked in.
For chipmakers, the calculus is shifting from maximizing China revenue to minimizing Washington blowback - a change that will reshape the global AI hardware market for years to come.
The sheer volume of approved chip exports - nearly a million advanced processors - has blindsided members of Congress who believed existing controls were far more restrictive.

Wall Street is now pricing in the reality that Nvidia's China business - once a growth engine - has become a political liability that could trigger regulatory crackdowns extending far beyond voluntary sales halts.
The company's MI300 series chips were included in the approved exports, and CEO Lisa Su now faces the same pressure Kress does to voluntarily restrict sales beyond what regulations require.
Now Congress has hard numbers showing just how many chips were cleared for export before that voluntary halt, and members from both parties are furious.
Some of those chips are now sitting in Chinese data centers, a fact that's driving the urgency behind Mast's legislative effort.

The Florida Republican is now leading a bipartisan effort to pass legislation that would shift the burden of proof in export licensing, requiring chipmakers to demonstrate that sales won't enhance Chinese military or surveillance capabilities rather than forcing the government to prove they will.

Brian Mast revealed today, igniting a Congressional push for legislation to dramatically tighten export controls. The disclosure comes as lawmakers scramble to contain fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal that's already reshaped Nvidia's leadership and sent shockwaves through the semiconductor industry. The sheer volume of approved chip exports - nearly a million advanced processors - has blindsided members of Congress who believed existing controls were far more restrictive. The Commerce Department signed off on selling more than 879,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, a number that's now driving urgent calls on Capitol Hill for a complete overhaul of America's semiconductor export regime. Brian Mast dropped the bombshell figure during hearings this week, revealing an approval volume that far exceeds what most lawmakers believed was flowing to China under current restrictions. Nvidia is still reeling from the departure of founder Jensen Huang amid a widening scandal, and interim CEO Colette Kress just announced the company would halt H200 chip sales to China entirely - a dramatic reversal that came despite White House approval. Now Congress has hard numbers showing just how many chips were cleared for export before that voluntary halt, and members from both parties are furious. The 879,000 figure represents approved sales from multiple chipmakers, with both Nvidia and AMD products included in the Commerce Department's green-lit shipments. Each chip represents compute capability that Beijing can deploy for applications Washington would rather it didn't have. Mast, who chairs a key subcommittee overseeing technology exports, didn't mince words about what the number means. The Florida Republican is now leading a bipartisan effort to pass legislation that would shift the burden of proof in export licensing, requiring chipmakers to demonstrate that sales won't enhance Chinese military or surveillance capabilities rather than forcing the government to prove they will. It's a fundamental restructuring of how America polices its most strategic technology exports. The legislative push arrives as Nvidia's stock has whipsawed investors through one of the most turbulent periods in the company's history. Kress delivered better-than-expected earnings in her first quarterly report as interim CEO, but the China export controversy has overshadowed those results. Wall Street is now pricing in the reality that Nvidia's China business - once a growth engine - has become a political liability that could trigger regulatory crackdowns extending far beyond voluntary sales halts. What's particularly alarming to national security hawks in Congress is the timeline. Many of these 879,000 chips were approved and shipped while the Huang scandal was already unfolding behind closed doors. Commerce Department officials were apparently clearing massive export licenses even as intelligence agencies were raising red flags about how previous chip shipments were being used. AMD finds itself caught in the same political crossfire, despite maintaining a lower profile than its larger rival. The company's MI300 series chips were included in the approved exports, and CEO Lisa Su now faces the same pressure Kress does to voluntarily restrict sales beyond what regulations require. It's a no-win situation for chipmakers: sell to China and face Congressional fury, or leave billions in revenue on the table to appease Washington. The broader semiconductor industry is watching nervously as chip giants have ignored calls for AI safety pauses and instead accelerated production to meet insatiable demand. Nvidia just completed its fastest product ramp ever with the H200, shipping thousands of units weekly before the China halt kicked in. Some of those chips are now sitting in Chinese data centers, a fact that's driving the urgency behind Mast's legislative effort. The Commerce Department hasn't commented on the specific 879,000 figure, but the number aligns with industry estimates of China-bound chip volumes over the past 18 months. What's changed is the political willingness to let those exports continue. The Huang scandal transformed the debate from a technical discussion about compute thresholds and end-use verification into a raw political fight about whether America is funding its own strategic competitor. The bill would create a presumption of denial for AI chip exports to China, require annual audits of all approved licenses, and impose criminal penalties on executives who knowingly facilitate diversions to military end users. The revelation that Commerce approved 879,000 AI chip sales to China has transformed what was already a crisis at Nvidia into a full-blown political reckoning for the entire semiconductor industry. Lawmakers who once trusted the export licensing process now see it as dangerously permissive, and they're moving fast to slam the door shut. For chipmakers, the calculus is shifting from maximizing China revenue to minimizing Washington blowback - a change that will reshape the global AI hardware market for years to come. What happens next depends on how quickly Congress can pass new restrictions and whether the industry will accept them or fight back.

Now Congress has hard numbers showing just how many chips were cleared for export before that voluntary halt, and members from both parties are furious.
The 879,000 figure represents approved sales from multiple chipmakers, with both Nvidia and AMD products included in the Commerce Department's green-lit shipments.
Each chip represents compute capability that Beijing can deploy for applications Washington would rather it didn't have.
Mast, who chairs a key subcommittee overseeing technology exports, didn't mince words about what the number means.

The Florida Republican is now leading a bipartisan effort to pass legislation that would shift the burden of proof in export licensing, requiring chipmakers to demonstrate that sales won't enhance Chinese military or surveillance capabilities rather than forcing the government to prove they will.
It's a fundamental restructuring of how America polices its most strategic technology exports.
The legislative push arrives as Nvidia's stock has whipsawed investors through one of the most turbulent periods in the company's history.
Kress delivered better-than-expected earnings in her first quarterly report as interim CEO, but the China export controversy has overshadowed those results.

Wall Street is now pricing in the reality that Nvidia's China business - once a growth engine - has become a political liability that could trigger regulatory crackdowns extending far beyond voluntary sales halts.
What's particularly alarming to national security hawks in Congress is the timeline.
Many of these 879,000 chips were approved and shipped while the Huang scandal was already unfolding behind closed doors.
Commerce Department officials were apparently clearing massive export licenses even as intelligence agencies were raising red flags about how previous chip shipments were being used.
AMD finds itself caught in the same political crossfire, despite maintaining a lower profile than its larger rival.
The company's MI300 series chips were included in the approved exports, and CEO Lisa Su now faces the same pressure Kress does to voluntarily restrict sales beyond what regulations require.
It's a no-win situation for chipmakers: sell to China and face Congressional fury, or leave billions in revenue on the table to appease Washington.
The broader semiconductor industry is watching nervously as chip giants have ignored calls for AI safety pauses and instead accelerated production to meet insatiable demand.
Nvidia just completed its fastest product ramp ever with the H200, shipping thousands of units weekly before the China halt kicked in.
Some of those chips are now sitting in Chinese data centers, a fact that's driving the urgency behind Mast's legislative effort.
The Commerce Department hasn't commented on the specific 879,000 figure, but the number aligns with industry estimates of China-bound chip volumes over the past 18 months.
What's changed is the political willingness to let those exports continue.

The Huang scandal transformed the debate from a technical discussion about compute thresholds and end-use verification into a raw political fight about whether America is funding its own strategic competitor.

The bill would create a presumption of denial for AI chip exports to China, require annual audits of all approved licenses, and impose criminal penalties on executives who knowingly facilitate diversions to military end users.
The revelation that Commerce approved 879,000 AI chip sales to China has transformed what was already a crisis at Nvidia into a full-blown political reckoning for the entire semiconductor industry.
Lawmakers who once trusted the export licensing process now see it as dangerously permissive, and they're moving fast to slam the door shut.
For chipmakers, the calculus is shifting from maximizing China revenue to minimizing Washington blowback - a change that will reshape the global AI hardware market for years to come.
What happens next depends on how quickly Congress can pass new restrictions and whether the industry will accept them or fight back.

extraction.body: The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, there had been 3.4 million requested sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices . "Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents. The Commerce Department, AMD and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment. "The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks continued. The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest." The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including Bytedance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu . The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China. In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries. Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS — Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions. "Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting. Maginfra and New Matrix did not immediately reply to requests for comment. Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers." CNBC did not independently verify this information. Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance. Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify. Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China. Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third controls. The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release. This is breaking news. The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including Bytedance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu .

The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China.

In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.

Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS — Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions.

sources.title: Commerce Approved 879K AI Chips to China, Sparking Congress Push
passages: The revelation that Commerce approved 879,000 AI chip sales to China has transformed what was already a crisis at Nvidia into a full-blown political reckoning for the entire semiconductor industry.

The Commerce Department signed off on selling more than 879,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, a number that's now driving urgent calls on Capitol Hill for a complete overhaul of America's semiconductor export regime.
It's a no-win situation for chipmakers: sell to China and face Congressional fury, or leave billions in revenue on the table to appease Washington.
Brian Mast dropped the bombshell figure during hearings this week, revealing an approval volume that far exceeds what most lawmakers believed was flowing to China under current restrictions.
Kress delivered better-than-expected earnings in her first quarterly report as interim CEO, but the China export controversy has overshadowed those results.
Nvidia just completed its fastest product ramp ever with the H200, shipping thousands of units weekly before the China halt kicked in.
For chipmakers, the calculus is shifting from maximizing China revenue to minimizing Washington blowback - a change that will reshape the global AI hardware market for years to come.
The sheer volume of approved chip exports - nearly a million advanced processors - has blindsided members of Congress who believed existing controls were far more restrictive.

Wall Street is now pricing in the reality that Nvidia's China business - once a growth engine - has become a political liability that could trigger regulatory crackdowns extending far beyond voluntary sales halts.
The company's MI300 series chips were included in the approved exports, and CEO Lisa Su now faces the same pressure Kress does to voluntarily restrict sales beyond what regulations require.
Now Congress has hard numbers showing just how many chips were cleared for export before that voluntary halt, and members from both parties are furious.
Some of those chips are now sitting in Chinese data centers, a fact that's driving the urgency behind Mast's legislative effort.

The Florida Republican is now leading a bipartisan effort to pass legislation that would shift the burden of proof in export licensing, requiring chipmakers to demonstrate that sales won't enhance Chinese military or surveillance capabilities rather than forcing the government to prove they will.

extraction.body: The Commerce Department approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, Rep. Brian Mast revealed today, igniting a Congressional push for legislation to dramatically tighten export controls. The disclosure comes as lawmakers scramble to contain fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal that's already reshaped Nvidia's leadership and sent shockwaves through the semiconductor industry. The sheer volume of approved chip exports - nearly a million advanced processors - has blindsided members of Congress who believed existing controls were far more restrictive. The Commerce Department signed off on selling more than 879,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, a number that's now driving urgent calls on Capitol Hill for a complete overhaul of America's semiconductor export regime. Brian Mast dropped the bombshell figure during hearings this week, revealing an approval volume that far exceeds what most lawmakers believed was flowing to China under current restrictions. Nvidia is still reeling from the departure of founder Jensen Huang amid a widening scandal, and interim CEO Colette Kress just announced the company would halt H200 chip sales to China entirely - a dramatic reversal that came despite White House approval. Now Congress has hard numbers showing just how many chips were cleared for export before that voluntary halt, and members from both parties are furious. The 879,000 figure represents approved sales from multiple chipmakers, with both Nvidia and AMD products included in the Commerce Department's green-lit shipments. Each chip represents compute capability that Beijing can deploy for applications Washington would rather it didn't have. Mast, who chairs a key subcommittee overseeing technology exports, didn't mince words about what the number means. The Florida Republican is now leading a bipartisan effort to pass legislation that would shift the burden of proof in export licensing, requiring chipmakers to demonstrate that sales won't enhance Chinese military or surveillance capabilities rather than forcing the government to prove they will. It's a fundamental restructuring of how America polices its most strategic technology exports. The legislative push arrives as Nvidia's stock has whipsawed investors through one of the most turbulent periods in the company's history. Kress delivered better-than-expected earnings in her first quarterly report as interim CEO, but the China export controversy has overshadowed those results. Wall Street is now pricing in the reality that Nvidia's China business - once a growth engine - has become a political liability that could trigger regulatory crackdowns extending far beyond voluntary sales halts. What's particularly alarming to national security hawks in Congress is the timeline. Many of these 879,000 chips were approved and shipped while the Huang scandal was already unfolding behind closed doors. Commerce Department officials were apparently clearing massive export licenses even as intelligence agencies were raising red flags about how previous chip shipments were being used. AMD finds itself caught in the same political crossfire, despite maintaining a lower profile than its larger rival. The company's MI300 series chips were included in the approved exports, and CEO Lisa Su now faces the same pressure Kress does to voluntarily restrict sales beyond what regulations require. It's a no-win situation for chipmakers: sell to China and face Congressional fury, or leave billions in revenue on the table to appease Washington. The broader semiconductor industry is watching nervously as chip giants have ignored calls for AI safety pauses and instead accelerated production to meet insatiable demand. Nvidia just completed its fastest product ramp ever with the H200, shipping thousands of units weekly before the China halt kicked in. Some of those chips are now sitting in Chinese data centers, a fact that's driving the urgency behind Mast's legislative effort. The Commerce Department hasn't commented on the specific 879,000 figure, but the number aligns with industry estimates of China-bound chip volumes over the past 18 months. What's changed is the political willingness to let those exports continue. The Huang scandal transformed the debate from a technical discussion about compute thresholds and end-use verification into a raw political fight about whether America is funding its own strategic competitor. The bill would create a presumption of denial for AI chip exports to China, require annual audits of all approved licenses, and impose criminal penalties on executives who knowingly facilitate diversions to military end users. The revelation that Commerce approved 879,000 AI chip sales to China has transformed what was already a crisis at Nvidia into a full-blown political reckoning for the entire semiconductor industry. Lawmakers who once trusted the export licensing process now see it as dangerously permissive, and they're moving fast to slam the door shut. For chipmakers, the calculus is shifting from maximizing China revenue to minimizing Washington blowback - a change that will reshape the global AI hardware market for years to come. What happens next depends on how quickly Congress can pass new restrictions and whether the industry will accept them or fight back.

extraction.body: Russia’s central bank plans to let ordinary investors trade bitcoin and other crypto on margin, capped at 300,000 rubles with a broker, a senior Bank of Russia official said this week, days after retail buying became legal. Olga Shishlyannikova, director of the central bank’s department of investment financial intermediaries, outlined the plan at the Ural Conference hosted by NAUFOR, the national association of securities market participants, RBC Investments reported. She said the margin rule and two other acts are under review at Russia’s Justice Ministry, and the regulator expects them to be registered by the end of 2026. It is not yet clear whether the 300,000-ruble margin limit for non-qualified investors will be shared with the existing cap on crypto purchases or counted separately. The central bank first published draft margin rules in July. Under that draft, brokers could accept cryptocurrencies as collateral for margin positions, and their clients could sell short. Both qualified and non-qualified investors would be able to trade on margin, with retail crypto trades subject to limits set by the Bank of Russia. Olga Shishlyannikova, director of the central bank’s department of investment financial intermediaries, outlined the plan at the Ural Conference hosted by NAUFOR, the national association of securities market participants, RBC Investments reported. She said the margin rule and two other acts are under review at Russia’s Justice Ministry, and the regulator expects them to be registered by the end of 2026. It is not yet clear whether the 300,000-ruble margin limit for non-qualified investors will be shared with the existing cap on crypto purchases or counted separately. The central bank first published draft margin rules in July. Under that draft, brokers could accept cryptocurrencies as collateral for margin positions, and their clients could sell short. Both qualified and non-qualified investors would be able to trade on margin, with retail crypto trades subject to limits set by the Bank of Russia. The draft also added crypto to the risk-coverage ratios brokers use to police leveraged trades. Those ratios set how far a broker can lend against a client’s portfolio and when positions are forcibly closed. Shishlyannikova also said the central bank expects the first Russian mutual funds that hold crypto directly to appear in 2027. Professional market participants have already filed applications to register such funds, she said. “Yes, we are considering the possibility next year of amending the relevant regulations to allow funds intended for qualified investors to buy cryptocurrency,” Shishlyannikova said. The regulator is not considering the same access for funds sold to non-qualified investors, she added. In late September, the central bank allowed fund managers to invest qualified investors’ money in cash-settled instruments tied to crypto prices, in a directive registered with the Justice Ministry. The proposed change would let those funds hold the coins themselves. Retail access to crypto futures will take longer. Deputy Governor Philipp Gabunia told reporters on Thursday that the Bank of Russia could let non-qualified investors trade crypto-linked futures once the spot market is running, if it sees no risks, Interfax reported. “For non-qualified investors, this could be a very sensitive story. Let’s launch, and now we’ll see how it starts to work,” Gabunia said. “If we don’t see risks, we’ll allow it. Non-qualified investors will have to be a little patient.” Gabunia said the market’s shape could still shift, including which coins are admitted and which derivatives are offered on them. “Legislation is now changing this configuration a lot,” he said. He said the central bank does not expect “super-large” turnover on Russia’s crypto market. Qualified investors can already trade futures tied to bitcoin, ether, Solana, XRP and Tron on Russian exchanges. Gabunia did not give a timeline for retail access. Russia’s law on digital currencies took effect Sept. 1, setting up rules for crypto trading through exchanges, brokers and trust managers, plus new crypto exchange offices and digital depositories. Qualified investors were cleared to buy crypto from that date. The comments fill in the next steps on a calendar that has moved quickly this month. Since Nov. 17, non-qualified investors in Russia have been able to buy bitcoin, ether and Tether’s USDT through brokers and crypto exchange offices, capped at 300,000 rubles a year per intermediary, or roughly $3,600. A separate central bank ordinance lets exchanges open organized crypto trading from Nov. 22, once the regulator approves their trading rules. Moscow Exchange, which is under U.S. sanctions, has said it plans to list bitcoin on Dec. 1, initially as a pilot. Watch live, catch up on episodes, and get exclusive content on the go. sources.title: Blacklisted Chinese universities procured Nvidia chips, records show
passages: At least six Chinese universities blacklisted by the US government have reported purchasing restricted Nvidia computer chips in recent years, a CNN review of business records found – highlighting US difficulties in controlling access to the in-demand technology.

A third university that’s part of the “Seven Sons” group, Beihang University in Beijing, also reported making more than a dozen purchases of Nvidia chips between 2022 and 2024, according to the records, mostly buying A100 and A800 chips.
Among the 90 buyers CNN examined, nearly 80% are universities, and nearly 14% are research institutes, while government agencies also bought some Nvidia chips.

“If you’re talking about who’s going to be investing in military AI capabilities in China, a lot of that would start at these universities.” The purchase notices had scant details about the supply chains that took the chips from Nvidia to the universities, or how the chips may be used there.
The number of universities involved and full scope of their Nvidia purchases have not been previously reported.
Two of those universities known for their ties to the Chinese military establishment reported buying the high-powered chips just in the last few months.

Concerns spiked over Chinese access to the technology as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week following the revelation he had a romantic relationship with a woman whose former company is suspected of helping smuggle chips into the country.

Most notable, experts said, was a procurement notice from September that Harbin Institute of Technology had purchased an A100 chip for about $7,000, and two notices in September and October that Northwestern Polytechnical University had bought four H200 chips for a total of about $240,000.
US regulations require Nvidia and other chip suppliers to determine the end user for chips they sell abroad, and to take various measures to avoid the chips getting into China.

“We know it happens, and it’s very difficult to stop.” The issue is likely to be a major talking point in this week’s high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping as the White House moves to close loopholes that have allowed sensitive, AI-powering computer chips into China.
CNN’s review was based on procurement documents from Chinese universities collected in a commercial database.
Experts said US officials were highly unlikely to approve sales that would go to a blacklisted university.
CNN was not able to verify whether the Nvidia hardware was delivered in each case described in the notices.
Under Chinese regulations, universities and other public entities are required to publish notices on their websites when they make certain purchases.

extraction.body: At least six Chinese universities blacklisted by the US government have reported purchasing restricted Nvidia computer chips in recent years, a CNN review of business records found – highlighting US difficulties in controlling access to the in-demand technology. Two of those universities known for their ties to the Chinese military establishment reported buying the high-powered chips just in the last few months. The number of universities involved and full scope of their Nvidia purchases have not been previously reported. The purchases, made through obscure sellers in China, were for relatively small amounts of older chips, not the industrial, cutting-edge computing technology that researchers fear could enable China to overtake the US in the artificial intelligence race. Still, they show how widely available restricted Nvidia chips remain inside China, and how difficult it is for the US to block the sale of the chips even to some of the most high-risk entities – a particularly sensitive concern following allegations linking Nvidia’s CEO to a potential Chinese intelligence asset. “Once these chips are in China, it’s very hard for anyone to be able to stop their sale,” said Kate Koren, a former US export control official who now serves as a research director at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “We know it happens, and it’s very difficult to stop.” The issue is likely to be a major talking point in this week’s high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping as the White House moves to close loopholes that have allowed sensitive, AI-powering computer chips into China. Concerns spiked over Chinese access to the technology as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week following the revelation he had a romantic relationship with a woman whose former company is suspected of helping smuggle chips into the country. Speaking to reporters last week, Mao Ning, a spokeswoman for China’s Foreign Ministry, said Beijing rejects US claims that restrictions on high-powered chips are necessary for US national security. “China firmly opposes the US overstretching the concept of national security and formulating various types of discriminatory lists to go after Chinese institutions,” she said. CNN’s review was based on procurement documents from Chinese universities collected in a commercial database. Under Chinese regulations, universities and other public entities are required to publish notices on their websites when they make certain purchases. Among the nearly 300 records CNN obtained and examined, most show purchases of Nvidia technology under US export control, such as A100, A800, H100, H200, and H800 chips. Among the 90 buyers CNN examined, nearly 80% are universities, and nearly 14% are research institutes, while government agencies also bought some Nvidia chips. Most notable, experts said, was a procurement notice from September that Harbin Institute of Technology had purchased an A100 chip for about $7,000, and two notices in September and October that Northwestern Polytechnical University had bought four H200 chips for a total of about $240,000. Both universities are part of a grouping known in China as the “Seven Sons of National Defense” because of their connections to China’s People’s Liberation Army. “Those are the universities that have tight linkages to the Chinese military,” said Gregory Allen, the CEO of Decision Tree Research, a firm focusing on tech and geopolitical issues. “If you’re talking about who’s going to be investing in military AI capabilities in China, a lot of that would start at these universities.” The purchase notices had scant details about the supply chains that took the chips from Nvidia to the universities, or how the chips may be used there. Both universities reported buying the chips not from Nvidia itself or a major supplier, but from little-known firms in China. Reuters previously reported on one of the Northwestern purchases. Under a new policy put in place last year after lobbying from Nvidia and Huang, the US government does allow the tech giant to sell the less powerful H200 chip to entities in China on a case-by-case basis – but those sales come with strict requirements related to reporting the end user of the chips. Experts said US officials were highly unlikely to approve sales that would go to a blacklisted university. Sales of the A100 chip to China are still banned – but before the US government put restrictions in place in 2022, the hardware was widely sold there. “It’s possible those were coming from stockpiles there before the controls were in place,” said Koren, because “there was a fairly large window of time” when the chips weren’t controlled under US export law. A third university that’s part of the “Seven Sons” group, Beihang University in Beijing, also reported making more than a dozen purchases of Nvidia chips between 2022 and 2024, according to the records, mostly buying A100 and A800 chips. The university has been blacklisted by the US since 2001. In addition to the universities with tighter military ties, three other universities on the US government’s “Entity List,” a blacklist of organizations that are banned from receiving shipments of controlled items without approval from federal officials, also reported purchases of high-end Nvidia chips in recent years. The records CNN obtained are likely incomplete because while public institutes in China are required to publicize procurement decisions, many only publish the notices locally or internally or take them down quickly. The commercial aggregator CNN used also doesn’t include all notices published by Chinese institutions. CNN was not able to verify whether the Nvidia hardware was delivered in each case described in the notices. US regulations require Nvidia and other chip suppliers to determine the end user for chips they sell abroad, and to take various measures to avoid the chips getting into China. It’s unclear how the universities’ suppliers acquired the chips. But in general, smuggling operations for these chips can be based on “very sophisticated shell companies, with shipments going from other countries to China, multiple hops, multiple currency changes, and falsified documents that make it much harder to detect,” Koren said. Government officials trying to disrupt this pipeline are facing a “constant” struggle to enforce bans, she said, “but rationally you have to know that despite your best efforts, some will get through.”

extraction.body: At least six Chinese universities blacklisted by the US government have reported purchasing restricted Nvidia computer chips in recent years, a CNN review of business records found – highlighting US difficulties in controlling access to the in-demand technology. Two of those universities known for their ties to the Chinese military establishment reported buying the high-powered chips just in the last few months. The number of universities involved and full scope of their Nvidia purchases have not been previously reported. The purchases, made through obscure sellers in China, were for relatively small amounts of older chips, not the industrial, cutting-edge computing technology that researchers fear could enable China to overtake the US in the artificial intelligence race. Still, they show how widely available restricted Nvidia chips remain inside China, and how difficult it is for the US to block the sale of the chips even to some of the most high-risk entities – a particularly sensitive concern following allegations linking Nvidia’s CEO to a potential Chinese intelligence asset. “Once these chips are in China, it’s very hard for anyone to be able to stop their sale,” said Kate Koren, a former US export control official who now serves as a research director at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “We know it happens, and it’s very difficult to stop.” The issue is likely to be a major talking point in this week’s high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping as the White House moves to close loopholes that have allowed sensitive, AI-powering computer chips into China. Concerns spiked over Chinese access to the technology as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week following the revelation he had a romantic relationship with a woman whose former company is suspected of helping smuggle chips into the country. Speaking to reporters last week, Mao Ning, a spokeswoman for China’s Foreign Ministry, said Beijing rejects US claims that restrictions on high-powered chips are necessary for US national security. “China firmly opposes the US overstretching the concept of national security and formulating various types of discriminatory lists to go after Chinese institutions,” she said. CNN’s review was based on procurement documents from Chinese universities collected in a commercial database. Under Chinese regulations, universities and other public entities are required to publish notices on their websites when they make certain purchases. Among the nearly 300 records CNN obtained and examined, most show purchases of Nvidia technology under US export control, such as A100, A800, H100, H200, and H800 chips. Among the 90 buyers CNN examined, nearly 80% are universities, and nearly 14% are research institutes, while government agencies also bought some Nvidia chips. Most notable, experts said, was a procurement notice from September that Harbin Institute of Technology had purchased an A100 chip for about $7,000, and two notices in September and October that Northwestern Polytechnical University had bought four H200 chips for a total of about $240,000. Both universities are part of a grouping known in China as the “Seven Sons of National Defense” because of their connections to China’s People’s Liberation Army. “Those are the universities that have tight linkages to the Chinese military,” said Gregory Allen, the CEO of Decision Tree Research, a firm focusing on tech and geopolitical issues. “If you’re talking about who’s going to be investing in military AI capabilities in China, a lot of that would start at these universities.” The purchase notices had scant details about the supply chains that took the chips from Nvidia to the universities, or how the chips may be used there. Both universities reported buying the chips not from Nvidia itself or a major supplier, but from little-known firms in China. Reuters previously reported on one of the Northwestern purchases. Under a new policy put in place last year after lobbying from Nvidia and Huang, the US government does allow the tech giant to sell the less powerful H200 chip to entities in China on a case-by-case basis – but those sales come with strict requirements related to reporting the end user of the chips. Experts said US officials were highly unlikely to approve sales that would go to a blacklisted university. Sales of the A100 chip to China are still banned – but before the US government put restrictions in place in 2022, the hardware was widely sold there. “It’s possible those were coming from stockpiles there before the controls were in place,” said Koren, because “there was a fairly large window of time” when the chips weren’t controlled under US export law. A third university that’s part of the “Seven Sons” group, Beihang University in Beijing, also reported making more than a dozen purchases of Nvidia chips between 2022 and 2024, according to the records, mostly buying A100 and A800 chips. The university has been blacklisted by the US since 2001. In addition to the universities with tighter military ties, three other universities on the US government’s “Entity List,” a blacklist of organizations that are banned from receiving shipments of controlled items without approval from federal officials, also reported purchases of high-end Nvidia chips in recent years. The records CNN obtained are likely incomplete because while public institutes in China are required to publicize procurement decisions, many only publish the notices locally or internally or take them down quickly. The commercial aggregator CNN used also doesn’t include all notices published by Chinese institutions. CNN was not able to verify whether the Nvidia hardware was delivered in each case described in the notices. US regulations require Nvidia and other chip suppliers to determine the end user for chips they sell abroad, and to take various measures to avoid the chips getting into China. It’s unclear how the universities’ suppliers acquired the chips. But in general, smuggling operations for these chips can be based on “very sophisticated shell companies, with shipments going from other countries to China, multiple hops, multiple currency changes, and falsified documents that make it much harder to detect,” Koren said. Government officials trying to disrupt this pipeline are facing a “constant” struggle to enforce bans, she said, “but rationally you have to know that despite your best efforts, some will get through.”

extraction.body: Nvidia, Export Controls, China, AI Hardware, AI Policy CNN reviewed about 300 procurement notices: at least six US-blacklisted Chinese universities reported buying restricted Nvidia chips. What is confirmed and what is not. Short answer: A CNN review of business records found that at least six Chinese universities on the US Entity List have reported buying restricted Nvidia chips in recent years, including two military-linked schools that reported purchases in the last few months, according to CNN's report of November 19, 2026 . The amounts are small and mostly older chips, bought from obscure Chinese sellers. CNN could not verify delivery, and it is unclear how the sellers got the chips. The finding widens a story we covered earlier this month. Reuters reported on November 11 that one blacklisted school, Northwestern Polytechnical University, bought H200 chips (see our Northwestern Polytechnical coverage ). CNN says the number of universities involved and the full scope of purchases have not been reported before. CNN highlights the cases experts called most notable: "Those are the universities that have tight linkages to the Chinese military," Gregory Allen of Decision Tree Research told CNN, adding that military AI investment would start at such schools. Export-chip control gate behind which a chip rests, representing restricted Nvidia chips reaching blacklisted universities Under Chinese rules, public bodies must publish notices when they make certain purchases. CNN used a commercial database that collects them. It examined nearly 300 records from about 90 buyers: nearly 80% universities, nearly 14% research institutes, and some government agencies. CNN excluded purchases of computing power from overseas data centres, a loophole the Trump administration moved this week to close with new regulations. The limits are significant, and CNN states them. The records are likely incomplete because many institutions only publish notices locally or take them down quickly. The database does not hold every notice. And CNN could not verify that the hardware was delivered in each case. The notices give scant detail on the supply chain or on how the chips would be used. The report does not claim smuggling. It says it is unclear how the sellers acquired the chips. Kate Koren, a former US export control official now at CSIS, offered a possibility: some A100 chips may come "from stockpiles there before the controls were in place," because for a time they were not controlled under US law. A100 sales to China are banned now, but they were widely sold before 2022. She also describes how smuggling networks can work: "very sophisticated shell companies" with multiple hops, currency changes and falsified documents. That is a general description, not a finding about these universities. For a claimed-versus-verified look at one smuggling allegation involving Nvidia executives, see our Muddy Waters GPU diversion explainer . Under a policy set last year after lobbying by Nvidia, the US allows the H200 to be sold to entities in China case by case, with strict requirements to report the end user, per CNN. Experts quoted say officials are highly unlikely to approve sales to a blacklisted university. The Entity List bars shipments of controlled items without federal approval (the license requirements sit in 15 CFR Part 744 of the Export Administration Regulations ), and US rules oblige Nvidia and other suppliers to determine the end user and avoid chips reaching China. So a university on the list buying an H200 through a local reseller does not match an approved sale. It does not tell us whether Nvidia or an authorised distributor did anything wrong. The report does not accuse Nvidia of selling to these buyers. Three points stand out for people who follow AI hardware. Because the whole story rests on these notices, it helps to know what they are. A Chinese public university that buys equipment above a set value must publish a notice, usually on its own procurement page or a government platform. The notice typically names the buyer, the item, the quantity, the price in yuan and the winning supplier. It rarely says where the supplier got the item, who will use it, or whether delivery happened. That is why the same record can support two stories. A cautious reading says a school ordered a chip and a reseller won the order. A stronger reading says restricted hardware reached a military-linked campus. The first is what the notice shows; the second needs proof of delivery and of the chip's path, which CNN did not have. Prices give a small clue: roughly $60,000 per H200 in the Northwestern Polytechnical notices, as CNN's totals imply, is the type of figure that suggests grey-market resale rather than a direct Nvidia sale, but that is our arithmetic on CNN's numbers, not a finding. Each step added buyers, not proof of a pipeline. The common thread is that the controls leave room at the retail edge of China's market, while large, cutting-edge shipments, which are the main worry, are harder to hide. Does this change what builders can buy? No. These are purchases inside China by blacklisted schools. Cloud and chip availability for ordinary buyers is not affected by this report. Will Nvidia be penalised? Nothing in the CNN report says so. Rules put the end-user check on suppliers, and enforcement is a Commerce Department matter. No action has been announced. Why do old chips matter? A100 and A800 are older, but they still train and run useful models. For a university lab that is enough to do real work, which is why the Entity List covers them. If you resell or procure accelerators, the practical lessons are plain. Check buyers against the Entity List before any sale. Keep an end-user record for each shipment. Be careful with intermediaries whose own supply trail you cannot see. A chip's journey can become a compliance question years later, as these notices show. We read CNN's full report (published November 19, 2026) and compared it with our earlier coverage of Reuters' November 11 report on Northwestern Polytechnical. We will update this post if the US government or Nvidia responds. Details are accurate as of November 19, 2026. Procurement records can change or be removed. On November 19, 2026 the House Foreign Affairs Committee used its Export Control Reform Act authority to publish Nvidia and AMD export license data for China. It says buyers requested 3.4 million AI chips as of May and Commerce approved more than 879,000. Here is what the committee said, what is still unclear and why it matters. Released November 18, 2026, the USCC annual report to Congress says China is evading export controls to obtain advanced semiconductors for PLA intelligentized warfare, while domestic chips still trail Nvidia and AMD. CNBC and Reuters highlight remote access through third-country data centers. Model Republic identified more than 400 coordinated accounts that defended Jensen Huang, attacked export-control advocates, and promoted Nvidia on X, Bluesky, and Reddit. The network traces to the Israeli influence firm Koios and a successor called IntellACT. Nvidia says it had no relationship with those firms and is trying to identify who ran the campaign.
